fixes.name: Bounded sequences; convergent sequences are bounded
fixes.what: The learner knows the definition of a bounded sequence (there is M with |a_n| <= M for all n, equivalently bounded above and below), can prove that every convergent sequence is bounded (use epsilon = 1 to bound the tail by |L| + 1, then take the maximum with the finitely many earlier terms), and uses the contrapositive to show that an unbounded sequence such as n diverges.
fixes.why: No point in this part defines a bounded sequence, yet p128, p129, p113, p116 and p121 all rely on it; p95 is where it naturally first appears.
Passing to the limit in the recursion uses that the shifted sequence (a_{n+1}) has the same limit as (a_n), which is taught in p87.
The conclusion that a monotone sequence converges exactly when it is bounded combines this result with the monotone convergence theorem.
Showing r^n diverges for r = -1 is the (-1)^n divergence proof from p93.
p119 places the Cauchy criterion alongside monotone convergence and the nested interval property as forms of completeness, which p108 establishes.

verdict: The part is sound and well ordered: proofs and examples are correct, the pieces fit together without real duplication, and the main gaps were unlinked needs between pieces plus a missing definition of a bounded sequence, now fixed. The remaining open needs (logic, induction, Archimedean property, triangle inequalities, supremum, completeness, nested intervals, binomial and geometric sums, irrationality of sqrt 2) belong to the foundations and real-number parts.
